papers.title: Domain Architecture Analysis Guides the Discovery of Unusual Glycyl Radical Enzyme Fusion Proteins
papers.label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.23.768175 v1

summary.one_liner: Sequence similarity network analysis of the glycyl radical enzyme superfamily uncovers a cluster of GRE/GRE-activating enzyme fusion proteins in photosynthetic eukaryotes, with one member characterized as an active pyruvate formate-lyase activated by its fused AE domain.
summary.plain: Enzymes that work without oxygen use a special radical, a reactive spot on a glycine building block, to carry out difficult chemistry. This paper sorts a large family of these enzymes by sequence similarity and finds an unexpected group in algae-like photosynthetic organisms in which the enzyme and its activating partner are joined into one protein. The authors show that one such fusion works as a pyruvate formate-lyase and that the attached activating part can install the radical on its own enzyme.
summary.why: It suggests oxygen-free radical chemistry may matter in ecologically important phototrophs such as diatoms, which were not previously expected to use it. The domain-architecture approach offers a general way to find new enzymes in large families, though the text does not establish how widespread these fusions are beyond the organisms studied.
summary.background:
- Enzymes: protein catalysts that speed up chemical reactions in cells.
- Glycyl radical enzymes (GREs): a class that uses a radical on a glycine residue, active mainly in oxygen-free environments.
- Radical: a molecule with an unpaired electron, very reactive.
- Activating enzyme (AE): a partner protein that creates the radical on the GRE; it is installed after the protein is made.
- Pyruvate formate-lyase: a classic GRE that breaks down pyruvate into formate and acetyl-CoA.
- Sequence similarity network: a map linking protein sequences by how similar they are, used to group families.
- Domain architecture: the arrangement of functional building blocks within a protein.
- Diatoms and microalgae: photosynthetic single-celled eukaryotes.
- Cryogenic electron microscopy: a method for imaging molecular structures at low temperature.

papers.abstract: Glycyl radical enzymes (GREs) use a post-translationally installed glycyl radical cofactor to catalyze chemically challenging reactions that are critical for anaerobic metabolism in microorganisms. Despite its importance, the GRE superfamily remains undercharacterized in part due to the vastness of its sequence space. Herein, we use sequence similarity network (SSN) analysis to survey the sequence diversity of the GRE superfamily and identify previously uncharacterized subfamilies. By analyzing the conserved domain architecture of each uncharacterized cluster, we find an unexpected cluster of GRE sequences from diverse photosynthetic eukaryotes. Bioinformatic, biochemical, and structural studies together demonstrate that these GREs have their catalytic subunits fused with a GRE-activating enzyme (GRE-AE). We characterize a highly expressed member of this subfamily as a functional pyruvate formate-lyase that is activated by its fused AE. Low resolution cryogenic electron microscopy confirms that this protein is a naturally occurring fusion, with a central dimeric GRE domain and one GRE-AE domain on each side. We further find that the GRE/GRE-AE fusion proteins are transcriptionally active in a wide range of diatoms and related microalgae. Overall, these findings uncover a previously unappreciated role for GRE-mediated anaerobic metabolism in ecologically important phototrophs, reveal that an attached AE can install a glycyl radical species on its cognate GRE, and show that domain architecture analysis is a powerful strategy to find novel enzymes among large enzyme superfamilies.

papers.title: RESUPER: a new computer program for identifying ordered regions, superposition ranges and conformational states in protein ensembles
papers.label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.22.768412 v1

summary.one_liner: RESUPER is a new program that splits NMR protein structure ensembles into rigid domains, picks a superposition range for each, and flags distinct conformational states, using a geometric split test and benchmarked against CYRANGE.
summary.plain: Protein structures solved by NMR are deposited as a bundle of many slightly different models, and their reported precision depends on which parts of the protein are lined up first. This paper presents RESUPER, a computer tool that finds the stable chunks (domains) of a protein, chooses which residues to line up for each chunk, and notices when the bundle contains more than one distinct shape. On test sets, it counted domains more accurately than the earlier CYRANGE method.
summary.why: Reported precision of NMR structures is often misleading when a protein has several domains or flexible regions, so a more transparent way to choose the alignment could make structure quality easier to judge. The approach is reported as integrated into the POKY tool with a graphical interface, but the text does not show how widely it will be adopted.
summary.background:
- NMR (nuclear magnetic resonance) structure determination yields an ensemble of many conformers, not one structure.
- Superposition means rotating and shifting models so chosen residues overlap; the precision number depends on that choice.
- A protein domain is a compact, semi-rigid region of a chain; rigid-body means parts that move together without bending.
- CYRANGE is an earlier two-stage method for choosing superposition ranges; RESUPER follows its approach but changes how domain splits are decided.
- Apo-Pin1 (PDB 7SA5) is a protein entry without a bound ligand, used here as a worked example.
- The paper reports statistical comparisons; the text says none of four post hoc comparisons on CYRANGE were significant.

papers.abstract: NMR structures are deposited as ensembles of conformers, and their precision is reported after superposition on a chosen set of residues, a choice that is difficult for proteins with several domains or flexible regions. We present RESUPER, a program that identifies rigid domains, selects a superposition range for each domain, and detects distinct conformational states in protein ensembles. RESUPER follows the two-stage method of CYRANGE, but each domain split is decided by a geometric test that can be checked on the structure. On two test sets fixed before evaluation, RESUPER counted the domains correctly in 95 of 96 and 45 of 48 ensembles (CYRANGE: 76 and 39) and put two separate rigid bodies into one range in 0 and 4 ensembles (CYRANGE: 17 and 9). On 222 randomly selected NMR entries, the two programs gave the same number of domains for 88% of the entries, and none of four prespecified comparisons, applied post hoc to CYRANGE, showed a statistically significant difference. For apo-Pin1 (PDB 7SA5), RESUPER found the two deposited conformational states. Analyzed separately, one state has a single superposition range covering both domains and the other has separate ranges. RESUPER is integrated into POKY with a graphical user interface.

papers.title: Resolving Hepatic Metabolic Flux During Ex Vivo Liver Perfusion Reveals Compartment-Specific Constraints
papers.label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.24.769061 v1

summary.background:
- Normothermic machine perfusion: keeping an organ warm and circulating fluid through it outside the body.
- Metabolic flux: the rate at which molecules are converted through biochemical pathways.
- 13C tracers: fuels (lactate, pyruvate, glucose) with heavy carbon atoms, so their path through cells can be followed.
- Isotopomers: versions of a molecule that differ in where or how many heavy atoms they carry.
- TCA cycle: the central energy-producing cycle in mitochondria; malate is one of its intermediates.
- Gluconeogenesis: the liver making new glucose from non-sugar precursors.
- Compartmentation: dividing a tissue into functional regions with different metabolic behaviour.
- Lobectomy: surgical removal of a lobe of the liver.
summary.one_liner: Using 13C-labelled tracers in staged ex vivo perfused mouse livers and serial lobectomies, the authors test whether a simple glucose-fragment flux model holds and find that a two-compartment model (glycolytic plus gluconeogenic) fits intracellular isotopomer data better than a one-compartment model, with partial agreement between the two flux estimates.
summary.plain: Surgeons keep donor livers alive outside the body on a perfusion machine and currently judge them with broad measures. This study asks whether tracking how labelled sugars and fuels move inside liver cells can give a more detailed picture of how the liver is working. In mouse livers, a simple one-region model failed to fit most data, especially for TCA cycle intermediates such as malate, while a model split into two cell regions fit 41 of 45 datasets.
summary.why: Better intracellular measures could eventually help judge whether a donor liver is healthy enough to transplant, though the text is limited to mouse work and does not show any clinical use. The finding that liver compartmentation limits whole-liver flux estimates matters for how such tracer studies are interpreted, and the authors say simplified models still support quantitative assessment.

papers.abstract: Normothermic machine perfusion (NMP) is used to preserve and assess donor livers, but current viability criteria rely on global measures that do not resolve intracellular metabolism, which would provide a more mechanistic measure of donor liver function. We combined staged ex vivo perfusion of mouse livers, serial lobectomy and 13C tracers ([U-13C3]lactate, [U-13C3]pyruvate and [U-13C6]glucose) to test whether glucose fragment-based flux models used in vivo describe intact hepatic metabolism. With intracellular metabolite isotopomers as constraints, a homogeneous one-compartment model failed to fit most datasets, and the lack of fit centered on TCA cycle intermediates such as malate. A two-compartment model, in which a glycolytic compartment takes up glucose from the sinusoidal pool, including glucose released by a gluconeogenic compartment, fitted 41 of 45 datasets. Flux partitioning between compartments depended on nutritional state, which influenced hepatic metabolism more than perfusate glucose. Nevertheless, glucose fragment and two-compartment flux estimates correlated (R2 = 0.68-0.89). Intracellular isotope tracing thus shows that hepatic compartmentation constrains whole-liver flux estimation, while supporting simplified models for quantitative assessment during perfusion.

papers.title: Albumin alleviates pressure overload-induced heart failure by improving mitochondrial homeostasis via PKA-LKB1-AMPK axis
papers.label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.21.768247 v1

summary.background:
- Heart failure: the heart pumps too weakly to meet the body's needs; it is common, deadly and costly.
- Serum albumin: the main protein in blood plasma, which carries molecules around the body and helps maintain fluid balance; low levels are a known warning sign in heart disease.
- Transverse aortic constriction (TAC): a surgical method that narrows the main artery from the heart to create pressure overload, a standard way to model heart failure in mice.
- Cardiac hypertrophy and fibrosis: enlargement of heart muscle cells and build-up of scar-like tissue, both signs of heart damage.
- Mitochondria: the cell's energy-producing structures; "mitochondrial homeostasis" means keeping them healthy and balanced.
- Fatty acid oxidation and oxidative phosphorylation: the processes by which cells burn fats and sugars to make energy.
- AMPK and LKB1, PKA: cellular signaling proteins that sense energy status and coordinate responses; the paper proposes they form a chain activated by albumin.
- Knockout mice (AKO): mice genetically engineered to lack the albumin gene, used to test whether the protein is needed.
summary.one_liner: In a mouse model of pressure-overload heart failure, recombinant mouse serum albumin improved cardiac function and mitochondrial energy metabolism, with the authors proposing a PKA-LKB1-AMPK signaling axis as the mechanism.
summary.plain: Heart failure is a condition where the heart cannot pump blood well, and patients with it often have low levels of albumin, the most common protein in blood. This study used mice whose hearts were put under extra pressure by constricting the aorta, and found that giving them recombinant (lab-made) mouse albumin improved heart function, reduced thickening and scarring of the heart muscle, and eased inflammation. Mice lacking albumin did worse, and the albumin treatment helped them too.
summary.why: Low albumin is already linked to worse outcomes in heart failure, so this work tests whether albumin is a cause rather than just a marker, and suggests a possible treatment direction. The evidence comes from mice and cultured heart cells only, so it does not show that albumin would work in patients; the abstract also gives no detail on dosing or clinical testing.

papers.abstract: Aims Heart failure (HF) is a global health challenge due to its high incidence, mortality, and socioeconomic burden. Despite medical advancements, HF prognosis remains poor, highlighting the need for enhanced understanding and treatment strategies. Serum albumin, a key circulatory protein, has gained attention as a biomarker in cardiovascular diseases. Low serum albumin levels are linked to HF incidence, progression, and prognosis, suggesting its regulatory role, though mechanisms remain unclear. This study aimed to elucidate the role of serum albumin in HF pathogenesis and investigate its potential therapeutic effects. Methods and results A mouse model of pressure overload-induced HF was established via transverse aortic constriction (TAC). Serum albumin levels were significantly decreased in HF mice. Administration of recombinant mouse serum albumin (rMSA) effectively restored serum albumin concentrations, improved cardiac systolic function, alleviated cardiac hypertrophy and fibrosis, and reduced inflammatory responses, collectively attenuating disease progression. In contrast, albumin-knockout (Alb-/-, AKO) HF mice displayed aggravated pathological manifestations compared with wild-type (WT) controls, whereas rMSA supplementation markedly ameliorated these impairments. In vitro experiments demonstrated that rMSA protected against phenylephrine (PE)-induced hypertrophy in cardiomyocytes. To elucidate the underlying mechanism, transcriptomic analyses of cardiac tissues revealed that albumin played a critical role in improving mitochondrial homeostasis. Experimental validation further demonstrated that albumin activated the PKA-LKB1-AMPK signaling axis, leading to improved mitochondrial respiratory function and oxidative phosphorylation, as well as enhanced mitochondrial quality control. These changes promoted fatty acid oxidation and optimized energy metabolism, thereby reversing the energy imbalance underlying cardiac dysfunction. Conclusion Our study suggests that serum albumin exerts a protective effect in HF by improving mitochondrial dysfunction and energy metabolism disorders, thus reversing energy imbalance and mitigating disease progression. These results support recombinant serum albumin as a promising therapeutic for HF, with its mechanism involving the critical improvement of mitochondrial homeostasis.

papers.title: Synthesis of Cellulose Nanofiber Hydrogel Beads from Typha angustifolia for the Immobilization of Protease
papers.label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.18.767499 v1

summary.background:
- Cellulose: the structural fiber of plant cell walls; cellulose nanofibers are very thin strands of it.
- Hydrogel: a water-filled, soft, net-like material; here the beads absorb about four times their weight in water.
- Immobilization: fixing an enzyme onto a solid support so it stays in place and can be reused.
- Protease: an enzyme that cuts proteins into smaller pieces.
- Covalent binding: attaching the enzyme by strong chemical bonds rather than loose contact.
- Specific activity: enzyme activity per milligram of protein; higher means more active.
- Half-life: how long the enzyme keeps half its activity under operating conditions.
- Glutaraldehyde and sodium periodate: chemicals used to crosslink and to introduce reactive groups.
summary.one_liner: Cellulose nanofibers extracted from the invasive aquatic plant Typha angustifolia were oxidized, blended with polyvinyl alcohol, and crosslinked into hydrogel beads that serve as a covalent support for immobilizing crude protease.
summary.plain:
Typha angustifolia is an invasive water plant that causes trouble for wetlands and irrigation channels. This study turned its fibrous cellulose into small water-swollen gel beads, then attached a crude protease (a enzyme that breaks down proteins) to them. The enzyme on the beads kept more activity over time and worked across a somewhat wider range of temperature and pH than the free enzyme.</plain>
<parameter name="why">It offers one way to put an invasive plant to use while making enzyme catalysts easier to reuse, which matters for industrial processes. The text reports only laboratory measurements, so practical or industrial value is not yet shown.

papers.abstract: Typha angustifolia, an invasive aquatic macrophyte, poses a persistent challenge to wetland and irrigation management, yet its cellulose-rich biomass represents an underexploited feedstock for value-added biomaterials. This study reports the synthesis of cellulose nanofiber (CNF) hydrogel beads from T. angustifolia and evaluates their performance as a support matrix for protease immobilization. Cellulose was isolated by chlorite delignification and alkaline treatment, oxidized with sodium periodate to introduce aldehyde functional groups, blended with polyvinyl alcohol (PVA), and crosslinked with glutaraldehyde to form hydrogel beads. The beads exhibited a high water-absorption capacity of 399.67 {plus minus} 0.53% and a mechanical strength of 1.27 MPa. Covalent immobilization of crude protease onto the beads increased specific activity nearly threefold, from 24.56 {plus minus} 0.39 U/mg for the free enzyme to 59.20 {plus minus} 1.06 U/mg for the immobilized enzyme, corresponding to a loading efficiency of 50.61%. The immobilized enzyme also displayed broadened thermal and pH optima, shifting from 40 {degree sign}C to 50 {degree sign}C and from pH 8.0 to 9.0, respectively, and an extended operational half-life from 4.40 h to 11.37 h. These findings support the valorization of invasive Typha biomass into a robust, biodegradable support system with potential application in industrial biocatalysis.

papers.title: AlphaFold-assisted design of a modular Laminin E8 Fragment Panel
papers.label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.20.768189 v1

summary.background:
- Laminins: large three-chain proteins (α, β, γ) that form a major part of basement membranes, the thin sheets that support tissues.
- Recombinant: made in engineered cells rather than extracted from animal tissue.
- E8 fragment: a shortened, functional piece of laminin that keeps its cell-adhesion activity.
- Integrins: cell-surface receptors that attach cells to the extracellular matrix.
- AlphaFold: an AI tool that predicts the 3D shape of proteins from their sequence, used here to guide the design of fragments.
- Isoform: a variant of the same protein built from a different combination of chains.
summary.one_liner: Using AlphaFold structure predictions, the authors optimize recombinant laminin E8 fragments and build a modular panel of interchangeable α, β and γ chains that can be combined to make all laminin isoforms, with the fragments shown to support adhesion of cells expressing their matching integrins.
summary.plain: Laminins are large protein assemblies that form part of the scaffolding around cells in tissues, but they are too big to make easily in the lab. This work uses an AI protein-structure tool, AlphaFold, to design smaller working pieces of laminin, called E8 fragments, that can be produced in cells in culture. The authors built a set of interchangeable pieces that can be mixed to form the different laminin versions, and reported that these pieces help cells stick to them when those cells carry the matching receptors.
summary.why: Having a readily made, mix-and-match set of laminin fragments could make it easier to study stem cells, organoids and the cell receptors (integrins) that grip laminin. The text does not report how widely these tools have been adopted or how they compare with existing laminin preparations, so their practical impact is still to be seen.

papers.abstract: Laminins are large, heterotrimeric glycoproteins that are a major structural component of basement membranes and the extracellular matrix. Although they are difficult to produce recombinantly because of their large size, a smaller fragment of the laminin heterotrimer that supports cell adhesion and cell migration, termed E8, can be recombinantly expressed. Here, we use AlphaFold to optimize laminin E8 fragments and design a panel of interchangeable laminin , {beta}, and {gamma} chains that can be combined to produce all isoforms recombinantly. These recombinant E8 fragments support adhesion of cells bearing their cognate integrins, and will be useful tools for stem-cell, organoid, and laminin-binding integrin biology research.

papers.title: RUBRIC: rapid quality assessment tool for RNA 3D structures
papers.label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.20.767675 v1

summary.background:
- RNA is a chain of nucleotides; each has a sugar (ribose), a phosphate backbone and a base.
- Base pairs are hydrogen-bonded partner bases; Leontis-Westhof classes describe how the two bases pair geometrically.
- Ribose "pucker" is the puckered shape of the sugar ring; backbone "suites" describe conformations of the chain between sugars.
- Cryo-EM is an imaging method that yields 3D molecular models at near-atomic detail; "resolution" indicates how fine the detail is (lower numbers are better).
- The PDB (Protein Data Bank) is the public archive of deposited 3D structures.
- Validation means automated checks that find implausible geometry before a model is published or reused.
summary.one_liner: RUBRIC is an open-source tool that annotates RNA base pairs and checks their geometry, ribose sugar puckers and backbone conformations in 3D RNA structural models, flagging ambiguous or distorted features.
summary.plain: Cryo-electron microscopy now produces very large RNA molecule models quickly, but the checks used to catch errors in those models have not kept up. This paper presents RUBRIC, a free program that examines each RNA base pair, sugar ring and backbone segment, and flags shapes that are distorted or cannot be clearly classified. The authors report that it processes a complete human ribosome in under a second and that its base-pair labels mostly agree with established annotation programs.
summary.why: Errors in deposited RNA structures can propagate into the databases used to train and test structure prediction methods, so better validation could matter for both structural biology and computational modelling. The text reports that flagged problems were reduced in higher-resolution models or after targeted refinement, but its wider impact on the PDB is not yet shown.

papers.abstract: Cryo-electron microscopy has transformed RNA structural biology, revealing increasingly large and complex structures at an unprecedented pace. However, validation methods have lagged behind, and deposited models can contain distorted base pairs, incorrect ribose puckers and backbone conformational outliers. Here, we introduce Rapid Unified Base-pair, Ribose and backbone Integrity Check (RUBRIC), an open-source program that combines RNA structural annotation with local validation of base pairs, sugars, and backbones. RUBRIC assigns Leontis-Westhof classes and identifies geometrically ambiguous pairs that cannot be confidently assigned to a single class. It scores unambiguous pairs against reference geometries for each type and class, identifying the parameters responsible for low scores. It also assigns backbone suites to known conformers, suggests target torsions for unassigned suites and flags incorrect ribose puckers. RUBRIC analyzes a complete human ribosome in under a second, with base-pair detection and classification consistent with leading annotation programs. These programs disagreed significantly more often on pairs RUBRIC flagged as ambiguous than on unambiguous pairs. The geometric problems flagged by RUBRIC were reduced in higher-resolution models of the same RNA or after refinement targeting the affected geometry, indicating that these problems are correctable. A PyMOL plug-in and machine-readable output support model building, correction before deposition and assessment of deposited structures before reuse. RUBRIC can therefore help improve RNA structures in the PDB and the datasets used to train and evaluate RNA structure prediction methods.

papers.title: A cytochrome P450 is essential for cardenolide biosynthesis in Chrysolina beetles
papers.label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.19.767920 v1

summary.background:
- Cardenolides: steroid-based defensive chemicals, also the class of compounds that includes digitoxin, a heart medicine.
- Steroid backbone: the four-ring carbon skeleton shared by cholesterol and related molecules; pregnenolone is an early member of this family.
- Cytochrome P450: a large family of enzymes that add oxygen to molecules, often at specific carbon positions.
- Hydroxylation: adding an –OH group to a carbon atom; C14 and C15 refer to specific carbon positions on the steroid ring.
- Biosynthetic intermediate: a molecule formed along the way to a final product.
- Gene silencing: switching off a gene to see what happens to the organism's chemistry.
- Isotope tracing: feeding labeled atoms to an organism to track which molecules are made from which.
- Active-site residue: an amino acid lining the enzyme's reaction pocket that shapes which reaction it favors.
summary.one_liner: A cytochrome P450 enzyme from the leaf beetle Chrysolina coerulans, CcCYP9Z273, converts pregnenolone to caraumbellogenin via C14-hydroxylation, an early step in beetle cardenolide biosynthesis, and one active-site residue controls whether C14 or C15 hydroxylation occurs.
summary.plain: Some beetles make cardenolides, chemicals related to the heart drug digitoxin, to defend themselves. This paper identifies an enzyme in one leaf beetle species that performs an early chemical step in making these compounds. Silencing the gene for the enzyme reduced the beetle's cardenolide production, and tracing labeled molecules suggested the product it makes, caraumbellogenin, is a real intermediate on the route.
summary.why: Cardenolides have been studied in plants for a long time, but how insects make them was not known, so this identifies a missing step. The finding that insects and plants use different enzyme families to reach a shared intermediate is of interest to researchers in natural product chemistry and drug-related biosynthesis, though the text does not show direct medical applications.

papers.abstract: Cardenolides are naturally occurring steroidal derivatives that function as chemical defense compounds. These natural products are also widely used in medicine, as exemplified by the use of digitoxin in treating cardiac disease. Although cardenolides are most widely known as plant-derived natural products, these compounds are also produced in certain beetle species. However, while the biosynthesis of cardenolides has been well-studied in plants, it is not known how insects produce these compounds. Here we report the identification of a cardenolide biosynthetic enzyme from the leaf beetle Chrysolina coerulans. This cytochrome P450, CcCYP9Z273, catalyzes an array of steroid oxidations, including the conversion of pregnenolone into caraumbellogenin through C14-hydroxylation. Gene silencing suggests that CcCYP9Z273 is essential for beetle cardenolide formation and isotope tracing experiments support caraumbellogenin as an on-pathway biosynthetic intermediate. Mutagenesis of CcCYP9Z273 identifies an active-site residue that controls the enzyme product selectivity between C14- and C15-hydroxylation. These findings establish an early step in beetle cardenolide biosynthesis and highlight how distinct enzyme families have been recruited in insects and plants to generate a shared intermediate in the biosynthesis of these important metabolites.

papers.title: A recombinant expression system for the Variant Surface Glycoproteins enables structural elucidation of challenging classes of trypanosome proteins
papers.label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.19.767849 v1

summary.background:
- Trypanosomes are parasites that cause sleeping sickness (T. brucei) and related animal diseases (e.g., T. vivax).
- Antigenic variation: the parasite changes its surface coat so antibodies made against earlier versions no longer work.
- VSGs (Variant Surface Glycoproteins) form the dense surface coat; there are thousands of variants.
- VRPs are VSG-related proteins, which are less well understood.
- Recombinant expression means producing a protein in a host cell line that is not the original organism.
- Crystal structure: a three-dimensional atomic map of a protein, obtained by X-ray diffraction of protein crystals.
- Post-translational modifications: chemical additions (such as sugars) made to proteins after they are assembled, which affect their shape and function.
- Class A VSGs form dimers (pairs); Class B VSGs form trimers (triplets).
summary.one_liner: The authors show that suspension HEK293 cells can produce trypanosome Variant Surface Glycoproteins (VSGs), validate the system with VSG2 and VSG3 crystal structures, and use it to solve structures of a T. brucei VRP (VSG1619) and a T. vivax VSG (F9WSW0).
summary.plain:
The African sleeping-sickness parasite survives in its host by constantly swapping the protein coat on its surface, so the immune system keeps chasing an outdated version. Many of these coat proteins are hard to make in the parasite itself, which has slowed the study of them. This paper reports using human kidney-derived HEK293 cells, grown in liquid culture, as a factory to produce these proteins, and then determining their three-dimensional shapes.</plain>
<parameter name="why">Knowing the shapes of these coat proteins helps explain how the parasite hides from immune attack, which is central to understanding the disease. The text suggests the approach could extend to more distant trypanosome species, but the practical reach beyond the proteins studied here is not shown.

papers.abstract: The African Trypanosome (Trypanosoma brucei) persists in the mammalian host by periodically altering its surface coat with antigenically distinct versions of the Variant Surface Glycoprotein (VSG). This process is called antigenic variation and produces repeated cycles of immune clearance and parasite VSG switching, leading to high morbidity and mortality in the absence of chemotherapeutic intervention. Elucidating how variant VSGs evade immune clearance is thus central to understanding trypanosomiasis. Progress in studying the large repertoire of thousands of VSG proteins has been hindered by the challenge of producing these coat proteins. Here we report the use of suspension HEK293 cells for this purpose, a system with robust yields that preserves many key elements of VSG structure and post-translational modifications, verified by expressing, purifying, and determining the crystal structures of the well-characterized proteins VSG2 and VSG3. We then applied this heterologous expression system to the production of several VSGs that had failed to express natively in T. brucei, including truncated VSG-Related Proteins (VRPs) from T. brucei and VSGs from T. vivax. This allowed for the determination of the structures of the T. brucei VRP VSG1619 as well as the VSG F9WSW0 from Trypanosoma vivax (T. vivax). The structure of VSG1619 shows similarities to the upper-lobe structures of B-class VSGs, but the monomers do not assemble into either the typical A-class dimer or B-class trimer in solution or in the crystals. The structure of T. vivax F9WSW0 is notable as a divergent member of the Class-A group that was developed from structures of T. brucei VSGs, with a canonical dimer but differences in fold, disulfide placement, and N-linked glycosylation. The described expression system provides additional insight into the family of VRPs and opens the door to general progress with the VSGs of more divergent trypanosome species through recombinant protein production.

papers.title: ppGpp regulates NAD-RNA decapping by Escherichia coli NudC and RppH
papers.label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.19.767904 v1

summary.background:
- RNA messages are copies of genes; their lifespan in a cell controls how much protein is made.
- A "5' cap" is a chemical group on the start of an RNA; NAD+ (a common metabolic cofactor) can serve as one in bacteria.
- "Decapping" means removing that cap, which typically marks the RNA for breakdown.
- Nudix hydrolases are enzymes that cut chemical bonds in molecules bearing nucleotide-like groups; RppH and NudC are two E. coli members.
- ppGpp is an "alarmone," a signal molecule bacteria produce during stress such as starvation.
- Competitive inhibition means a molecule blocks the enzyme's active site, competing with the normal target.
- Crystal structures are atomic-resolution 3D models of proteins bound to ligands.
summary.one_liner: In E. coli, the Nudix hydrolase RppH is shown to remove NAD+ caps from RNA, and the alarmone ppGpp is shown to inhibit NAD-RNA decapping by both RppH and NudC, with crystal structures of NudC bound to NADH and ppGpp.
summary.plain: Cells attach small molecules to the front end of some RNA messages, and this "cap" affects how long the RNA survives. This paper reports that a bacterial enzyme called RppH can strip off the NAD+ cap, in addition to its known job on other RNA ends. It also finds that ppGpp, a small signaling molecule that bacteria make under stress, slows this stripping by two enzymes, and the authors show structures suggesting ppGpp blocks NudC's active site.
summary.why: It suggests a link between RNA stability and the stress-signaling molecule ppGpp, which may help explain how bacteria adjust gene expression when under stress. The text does not show what this means for cell survival or for other organisms, so the wider significance is uncertain.

papers.abstract: The regulatory landscape of RNA includes diverse non-canonical 5' cap structures, including Nicotinamide Adenine Dinucleotide (NAD+). In E. coli, the NAD cap and its cognate decapping enzyme NudC have provided important insight into NAD+-capped RNA stability; however, broader regulatory control of NAD-capped RNA degradation has remained unclear. Here, we demonstrate that the E. coli Nudix hydrolase RppH, known to act on 5' triphosphorylated RNA, also functions as an NAD+-decapping enzyme. RppH removes NAD caps from both linear and structured (hairpin) RNA substrates, revealing a previously unrecognized role in NAD+-RNA metabolism. These findings suggest that RppH may function alongside NudC to regulate the stability of NAD-capped transcripts. We further establish a direct relationship between NAD-RNA turnover and the alarmone ppGpp. Quantitative inhibition assays demonstrate that ppGpp inhibits decapping of NAD+-RNA by both NudC and RppH and indicate coordinated regulation of NAD-RNA decay during stress conditions. To provide a structural basis for these observations, we determined crystal structures of NudC bound to NADH and ppGpp. These structures reveal that ppGpp occupies the NudC active site, supporting a competitive inhibition mechanism. Together, our findings identify RppH as a novel NAD+-decapping enzyme and establish ppGpp as a regulator of NAD-RNA decay pathways, linking RNA capping and metabolic stress signaling.

papers.title: SAM-Dependent Precursor Peptide Engagement by Darobactin Maturase DarE
papers.label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.17.767387 v1

summary.background:
- RiPPs (ribosomally synthesized and post-translationally modified peptides): small peptides made by ribosomes and then chemically modified; many become drugs or antibiotics.
- Radical SAM enzymes: enzymes that use an iron-sulfur cluster and S-adenosylmethionine (SAM, a common cofactor) to make radical chemistry possible.
- RRE (RiPP recognition element): a separate protein module that many such enzymes use to bind their peptide; DarE lacks one.
- Darobactin: an antibiotic whose structure contains C-C and C-O-C crosslinks installed by DarE.
- HDX-MS: a method that measures how fast backbone hydrogens swap with deuterium from water; regions that are shielded (for example by binding) swap more slowly. Anaerobic use protects oxygen-sensitive iron-sulfur clusters.
- EPR spectroscopy: a technique that detects unpaired electrons and reports on the local chemical environment of metal clusters.
summary.one_liner: Using anaerobic hydrogen-deuterium exchange mass spectrometry and EPR spectroscopy, this study maps how the RRE-free radical SAM maturase DarE engages its precursor peptide DarA, and finds that the cofactor SAM contributes to peptide binding.
summary.plain: Bacteria make some antibiotics by first building a peptide chain and then having an enzyme stitch parts of it together with chemical crosslinks. This paper looks at how the enzyme DarE grabs its peptide partner, DarA, in the making of the antibiotic darobactin. The authors used a method that tracks which parts of the protein and peptide become shielded when they bind, and found that a region at the front of the enzyme, plus the leader part of the peptide, come together, with extra shielding only when the cofactor SAM is present.
summary.why: Most enzymes of this family use a separate helper module to recognise their peptide, but DarE does not, so the paper offers a different recognition route that may apply to other RRE-free enzymes. The text does not establish how general this mechanism is beyond DarE, and the study is limited to a single enzyme-peptide pair.

papers.abstract: Radical S-adenosylmethionine (SAM) enzymes that synthesize structurally constrained ribosomally synthesized and post-translationally modified peptides (RiPPs) with therapeutic potential mostly do so by employing a dedicated RiPP recognition element (RRE). With the growing number of RRE-free maturases discovered, how these enzymes engage their substrates remains largely unexplored. In this work, we mapped substrate-enzyme interactions in DarE, an RRE-free radical SAM enzyme that installs the C-C and C-O-C crosslinks of the antibiotic darobactin during the first step of darobactin biosynthesis. Using anaerobic hydrogen-deuterium exchange mass spectrometry (HDX-MS), we simultaneously resolved specific regions within the enzyme and its precursor peptide substrate, DarA, across five complex states. The N-terminal extension and part of the TIM-barrel domain of DarE, along with the leader region of DarA, become protected, revealing the peptide-engagement interface. Additional protection emerged only in the presence of SAM, identifying SAM as a key contributor to precursor-peptide engagement in an RRE-free RiPP maturase. Electron paramagnetic resonance spectroscopy further demonstrated precursor peptide-dependent perturbations of the chemical environment of the iron-sulfur clusters. These findings suggest that SAM-dependent peptide engagement, mediated in part by the N-terminal extension of the radical SAM enzyme, provides an alternative mechanism for precursor-peptide recognition in RRE-free RiPP maturases. Our work also demonstrates the utility of anaerobic HDX-MS for characterizing protein-peptide-small molecule interactions in oxygen-sensitive metalloenzymes.

papers.title: Unexpected properties of nucleotide condensates could facilitate the RNA world
papers.label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.18.767475 v1

summary.background:
- RNA world hypothesis: the idea that RNA came before DNA and proteins, carrying both genetic information and some catalysis.
- Biomolecular condensate: a droplet that forms by molecules separating from water, like oil in vinegar, without a membrane around it.
- Hydrolysis: water breaking a chemical bond; RNA's backbone is vulnerable to this, especially in acid.
- Ribozyme: an RNA molecule that catalyses a chemical reaction. The hammerhead ribozyme cuts RNA; religation is the reverse, joining the pieces back together.
- Divalent cations: positively charged metal ions with a 2+ charge, such as magnesium, that bridge negatively charged phosphate groups.
- Coarse-grained simulation: a simplified computer model that represents groups of atoms as single beads to study large-scale behaviour.
summary.one_liner: Nucleotides such as ATP, mixed with divalent cations and a short-chain alcohol or diol in water, form liquid condensates that concentrate RNA and DNA, protect RNA from acid hydrolysis, and shift a hammerhead ribozyme reaction from cleavage toward religation.
summary.plain: This paper asks how the earliest RNA-based life could have been kept apart from its surroundings before cell membranes existed. The authors report that simple nucleotide molecules, such as ATP, form droplet-like liquid compartments when mixed with metal ions and a small alcohol in water. Inside these droplets, RNA lasted for days under acidic conditions where it would normally break down quickly, and a ribozyme (an RNA that acts as an enzyme) reacted in the reverse direction.

papers.abstract: A key question in the RNA world hypothesis for the origin of life is the nature of the compartment that separates and protects the RNA from its environment. While membranes are a leading candidate for the initial compartment, biomolecular condensates have been proposed as an alternative, possibly simpler route to compartments. Here we show that bona fide liquid condensates form spontaneously when nucleotides (such as ATP) are mixed with divalent cations and a short-chain alcohol or diol in water. These condensates do not require any polymer to form, but can concentrate polymers like RNA and DNA, which show unexpected chemical behavior inside the condensates. Most surprisingly, RNA survives for days inside nucleotide condensates under acidic conditions that cause rapid and extensive hydrolysis in bulk. This effect is also observed for a phosphate-ester model substrate and therefore likely reflects the suppression of backbone cleavage. Coarse-grained simulations suggest that the condensate interior is bound together by magnesium-phosphate bridging interactions and is therefore highly depleted of water. At neutral pH, the same compartment reverses the course of a hammerhead ribozyme reaction, shifting it from cleavage toward religation. Finally, we observe that nucleotide droplets also spontaneously organize phospholipids at their surface, suggesting a possible evolutionary route from biomolecular condensates toward membranes. Thus, we believe that nucleotide condensates, which are built from the same building blocks as the genetic polymers themselves, overcome long-standing challenges with the RNA world hypothesis for the origin of life by protecting nucleic acids and reshaping their chemistry.

papers.title: Wilson disease mechanisms manipulate ATP7B activity
papers.label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.16.766959 v1

summary.background:
- Copper is needed by enzymes but is toxic when unregulated.
- ATP7B is a P-type ATPase: a membrane pump that uses energy (ATP) to push metal ions across membranes.
- Wilson disease is caused by variants (mutations) in the ATP7B gene.
- Cryo-EM: a method that images frozen molecules to build 3D atomic structures.
- Nanodiscs: small lipid bubbles that hold a membrane protein in a membrane-like setting.
- Inward- and outward-facing conformations: the pump's two shapes, open to the cell interior or to the outside, alternating during transport.
- Salt bridge: an attraction between oppositely charged amino acids that helps hold a protein shape.
- Coarse-grained molecular dynamics: simplified computer simulations of how molecules move over time.
- Metal-binding domains: protein regions that grab copper ions and pass them along.
summary.one_liner:
A cryo-EM structure of human ATP7B in lipid nanodiscs, combined with coarse-grained simulations and mutagenesis, maps how Wilson disease variants (notably R969Q and W939C) disrupt a salt bridge, a cholesterol-binding site, and metal-binding domain dynamics in this copper transporter.</one_liner>
<parameter name="plain">Wilson disease is an inherited condition in which the body cannot get rid of extra copper, so the metal builds up in the liver, brain and other organs. This paper studies the ATP7B protein, a pump that moves copper and sends excess into bile, and asks how disease-linked mutations break it. The authors used a high-resolution 3D structure of the protein plus computer simulations and lab tests to find the specific parts that the mutations disturb.
summary.why: Current Wilson disease treatments mainly lower total copper, so a drug that repairs the faulty pump itself would be a different approach. The structural map of how particular mutations disrupt the protein could guide the design of pharmacological chaperones (small molecules that help a misfolded protein work), though the text does not show any such drug was tested.

papers.abstract: Copper is an essential cofactor for enzymes involved in diverse processes including mitochondrial respiration and the metabolism of neurotransmitters, collagen and melanin. However, its redox activity requires tight homeostatic control. The P-type ATPases ATP7A and ATP7B help deliver copper to cuproenzymes, and ATP7B mediates the excretion of excess copper into bile. Pathogenic ATP7B variants cause Wilson disease (WD), leading to copper accumulation in organs including the liver, kidney, and brain, and to disruption of copper-dependent processes. Current treatments primarily reduce systemic copper levels, while emerging gene therapies aim to restore ATP7B function. A complementary therapeutic strategy would be to rescue dysfunctional ATP7B using pharmacological chaperones, but their development is limited by an insufficient understanding of how WD variants perturb ATP7B structure and function. Here, we present a cryo-EM structure of human ATP7B reconstituted in lipid nanodiscs together with coarse-grained molecular dynamics simulations, as well as mutagenesis, functional and sequence analyses. We identify a salt bridge (E754-R969), crucial for the transition between inward- and outward-facing conformations, which is abolished by the R969Q disease variant. Additionally, we find a conserved stabilizing cholesterol-binding site severely disrupted by the WD variant W939C. Furthermore, we present new insights into the dynamics of metal binding domains 5 and 6 hinting at a copper relay mechanism in ATP7B. Together, these findings reveal lipid- and domain-mediated mechanisms of ATP7B regulation and explain how specific WD variants disrupt them, providing a structural framework for mutation-directed therapeutic strategies, including pharmacological chaperones.

papers.title: Paired Deep Mutational Scanning of Lck Activity and Inhibitor Sensitivity Enables the Engineering of Pharmacological Control of T Cell Receptor Signaling
papers.label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.13.766442 v1

summary.background:
- Kinases are enzymes that add phosphate groups to other proteins, acting as switches in cell signaling.
- Lck is a kinase essential for T cell receptor signaling, the pathway by which T cells recognize targets.
- Deep mutational scanning: a method that makes and tests very large numbers of protein variants in parallel to see which changes matter.
- Reversible inhibitors bind a protein and can be removed; the drugs here (dabrafenib, erlotinib, gefitinib, imatinib, nilotinib) are approved for other diseases.
- Allosteric: affecting a protein's activity from a site far from where the drug or ligand binds.
- Jurkat cells: a standard immortalized T cell line used in laboratory experiments.
- IL-2: a signaling molecule T cells produce when activated.
summary.one_liner: Deep mutational scanning of full-length Lck kinase maps how nearly all single amino acid changes affect its activity and its sensitivity to five approved reversible inhibitors, yielding a nilotinib-sensitized variant (I312S) that can be switched off by drug in T cells.
summary.plain: Scientists wanted a way to switch off a specific signaling enzyme in immune cells using an ordinary drug, without breaking the enzyme's normal job. They tested nearly every single-letter change in one part of the enzyme Lck and measured how each change affected its activity and how easily five approved drugs could block it. One variant, I312S, kept working in T cells and was shut down selectively by nilotinib, reducing its signaling and interleukin-2 output.
summary.why: The approach offers a general route to making engineered signaling proteins drug-controllable, which may matter for designing cell-based immunotherapies that can be dialed up or down. The text reports the effect in Jurkat cells only, so its relevance to therapy in patients is not established here.

papers.abstract: Controlling signaling enzymes with small molecules is a central goal in chemical biology and is of great utility for engineering cell-derived immunotherapies. Yet strategies for conferring selective small-molecule sensitivity without disrupting a protein's native function remain limited. Here we present a generalizable approach to engineering small molecule-controlled multidomain protein kinases. Using deep mutational scanning of full-length Lck, a tyrosine kinase essential for T cell receptor (TCR) signaling, we measured the effect of nearly all single amino acid substitutions in the kinase domain on phosphotransferase activity. The resulting activity landscape defined the domain's tolerance to substitution, mapped the regulatory interfaces that tune phosphotransferase activity, and, by treating bulky substitutions as ligand proxies, nominated cryptic pockets where covalent liganding is predicted to allosterically inhibit Lck. In parallel screens, we measured the sensitization of each variant to five clinically approved, reversible drugs: dabrafenib, erlotinib, gefitinib, imatinib, and nilotinib. Together, these landscapes identified substitutions that preserved or enhanced activity while sensitizing Lck to inhibition. Sensitizing substitutions were distributed throughout the kinase domain, including positions more than 30 [A] from the ATP-binding site, implicating long-range allosteric networks linking distal perturbations to ATP-binding site conformation and inhibitor potency. Integrating the activity and sensitization landscapes yielded a nilotinib-sensitized variant, I312S, that supports TCR signaling and, upon drug treatment, selectively suppresses proximal signaling and IL-2 production in Jurkat cells even in the presence of endogenous Lck.

papers.title: Cryo-EM structure of plant ABCC1 reveals mode of arsenic transport
papers.label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.16.767027 v1

summary.background:
- ABC transporters: membrane proteins that use energy from ATP to move molecules across cell membranes.
- Vacuole: a storage compartment inside plant cells where waste and toxins can be sequestered.
- Phytochelatins (PCs): short peptides that bind heavy metals; PC2 and PC3 are versions with two and three units.
- Arsenic(III): a toxic form of arsenic that binds strongly to sulfur atoms.
- ATPase activity: the rate at which a protein breaks down ATP to power transport; used here as a readout of function.
- Cryo-EM: an electron microscopy method that images frozen molecules to reconstruct their three-dimensional atomic structure.
- Apo state: the protein without any bound substrate.
- Note: the abstract text is missing the co-factor after "in the presence of", so the exact assay conditions cannot be stated.
summary.one_liner: Cryo-EM structures of maize ABCC1, a plant vacuolar transporter, in apo form and bound to a PC2-As(III) complex, with ATPase assays showing how phytochelatin chain length affects transport.
summary.plain: Plants can trap toxic heavy metals such as arsenic by binding them to small peptides called phytochelatins and then pumping the complexes into a storage compartment inside the cell. This paper uses a very high-resolution imaging method to look at the maize pump protein, ABCC1, both empty and holding an arsenic-peptide complex. The authors show where the arsenic sits and which protein residues help hold it.
summary.why: Knowing exactly how this pump grabs arsenic could help plant scientists think about engineering crops that tolerate contaminated soil, though the text itself does not test any crop. The work is a structural study, so its practical value is still speculative.

papers.abstract: Plant ATP-binding cassette transporter C1 (ABCC1) mediates the vacuolar sequestration of heavy metal-phytochelatin (PC) complexes for cytosolic detoxification, yet the structural mechanisms of substrate recognition and metal coordination remain uncharacterized. Here, we report functional assays and single-particle cryo-EM structures of maize ABCC1 (ZmABCC1) in its apo state and bound to an PC2-As(III) complex. Functional assays demonstrate that ZmABCC1 ATPase activity is sequentially increased by glutathione, PC2, and PC3 in the presence of , supporting that longer PC chain lengths increase transport efficiency. The substrate-bound structure reveals the mode of substrate binding of the heavy metal complex, with the As(III) atom coordinated in a trigonal pyramidal geometry by three sulfur atoms from two PC2 ligands. Arg1200 plays a key role through nonpolar interaction with As(III) through its aliphatic side chain and an electrostatic interaction with the carboxyl group of PC2. These results define the molecular basis of PC-mediated heavy metal transport by plant ABCC1 which could be utilized to inform efforts to engineer crop stress resilience.

papers.title: IMPRESS: AI-coupled HPC workflows for protein design
papers.label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.13.766417 v1

summary.background:
- Protein design: inventing amino-acid sequences and 3D shapes that fold and perform a chosen function.
- Backbone: the main chain of a protein's 3D structure, generated first by a generative model.
- Inverse folding: predicting a sequence that would fold into a given backbone shape.
- Structure predictor: a model that estimates the 3D shape a sequence will fold into.
- Active-site motif: the few residues in an enzyme that do the chemistry; "discontinuous" means they are far apart in the sequence.
- Binder: a molecule or protein that attaches to a target; PDZ domains are a common protein-binding module.
- In silico: done by computer simulation or prediction, not in a physical experiment.
- HPC workflow: software that runs many compute-heavy jobs across a high-performance computing cluster, here asynchronously.
summary.one_liner: IMPRESS is a runtime framework in which chained AI protein-design pipelines (backbone generation, inverse folding, structure prediction) adaptively halt, resample, or branch based on their own results, evaluated asynchronously, and is tested on enzyme active-site motifs, small-molecule binder design, and PDZ binder redesign using in silico metrics.
summary.plain: Designing new proteins with AI usually runs a fixed chain of models, where each stage filters candidates and the effort split between stages is set in advance. This paper describes IMPRESS, a system where each design pipeline can change its own course while it runs, such as trying more of the cheap steps or branching into new searches. The authors report that this helped on some hard enzyme-site problems that the fixed chain could not solve, though all their comparisons are computer-based predictions rather than lab experiments.
summary.why: Fixed pipelines can only discard candidates and may find nothing for targets far from what the AI models were trained on, so a way to redirect effort at runtime addresses a real limitation. The claims rest on in silico metrics only, and the authors themselves expect the benefit to matter most for distant targets, which they have not shown experimentally.

papers.abstract: Protein design campaigns are often run as multi-stage pipelines with a generative backbone model, an inverse-folding model, and a structure predictor chained together in that order. The stages differ by one to two orders of magnitude in cost per candidate, and the allocation of sampling effort across them is fixed before a campaign begins. Such a filter cascade can only discard candidates. It cannot redirect sampling toward the regions of design space a model stack can reach, and for targets whose constraints are far from the generative model's training distribution it may return no solution at any practical sample count. We present IMPRESS (Integrated Machine-learning for PRotein Structures at Scale), a framework in which design pipelines are stateful objects that halt, continue, resample, or branch at runtime from their own accumulated results. Adaptive decisions are evaluated asynchronously with respect to execution, so a campaign refines itself without global synchronization. We apply IMPRESS to three problems: backbone generation on discontinuous enzyme active-site motifs, de novo small molecule binder design, and PDZ binder redesign. Adaptive parameterization solves active-site motifs carried on three or more discontinuous residue islands that a fixed cascade does not solve, shifts the realized task mix toward inexpensive sequence exploration, and produces sequence ensembles that explore broadly but stay near their inputs. All comparisons reported here are between in silico metrics. We expect that adaptive parameterization will matter most for targets furthest from the training distributions of the underlying models, and that the same primitives will accommodate experimental measurement as a steering signal.

papers.title: Actin Assembly on Biomimetic Lipid-coated and Functionalized Bead Surfaces
papers.label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.11.765950 v1

summary.background:
- Actin: a protein that forms long filaments, the main scaffolding that pushes cell edges forward.
- Arp2/3 complex: a protein assembly that starts new actin branches from existing filaments.
- Capping protein (CP): a protein that caps the ends of filaments and stops them growing; regulators can switch it off.
- WASP/WAVE and CARMIL proteins: membrane-bound regulators that activate Arp2/3 and capping protein at the right place and time.
- Reconstitution: rebuilding a biological process from purified parts outside the cell to see what each part does.
- Biomimetic: designed to imitate a natural structure, here a cell membrane, using simple materials.
- Functionalized beads: beads with chemical groups attached so that proteins can be anchored to them.
summary.one_liner: This methods paper describes a bead-based biomimetic system, with lipid- or glutathione-coated surfaces, for reconstituting Arp2/3-driven actin nucleation and capping protein regulation, along with protocols for imaging and quantifying the resulting actin networks.
summary.plain: Cells move partly by building networks of protein fibers (actin) at their outer membrane, and this work describes a way to rebuild that process in a test tube. The researchers coat small beads with fat-like lipids or a chemical tag, attach the proteins that switch actin growth on and off, and then watch and measure the fiber networks that form under a microscope. The text presents this as a set of step-by-step protocols rather than reporting new findings.
summary.why: A controlled, purified version of the cell's membrane machinery lets researchers test how specific regulators change actin assembly, without the full complexity of a living cell. The text does not report specific results, so its usefulness depends on how well the protocols work for other labs, which it does not show.

papers.abstract: Dynamic assembly of actin filaments drives cell protrusion and other aspects of cell motility. Reconstitution of actin assembly from purified components is a powerful approach for understanding the molecular mechanisms that underlie these processes. Purified preparations of actin, actin-binding proteins, and regulators of actin-binding proteins enable a broad spectrum of reconstitution experiments. Much of this actin filament assembly occurs at the plasma membrane, with exquisite temporal and spatial regulation. We developed a biomimetic reconstitution system using purified lipids or glutathione on the surface of functionalized beads as models for actin assembly at the plasma membrane. The system incorporates two critical pathways for regulation of actin assembly: nucleation of actin polymerization by Arp2/3 complex and activation of heterodimeric actin capping protein (CP). Arp2/3 complex and CP are both essentially inactive in the basal resting state of the cytoplasm. The system incorporates membrane-bound activators for Arp2/3 complex, such as WASP and WAVE family proteins, and for CP, such as CARMILs and other CPI-motif proteins. Membrane-bound components are coupled to beads either through lipids, which allow lateral mobility, or through glutathione groups attached to the bead surface via flexible linkers. Fluorescence microscopy of labeled components, combined with quantitative image analysis, is used to assess the combined effects of the regulators and thereby test molecular mechanisms for regulation of actin assembly. Here, we describe protocols for preparing functionalized beads, coupling regulators to the bead surface, performing actin assembly reactions, and imaging and quantifying the resulting actin networks.

papers.title: Structural basis of SBDS dysfunction in Shwachman-Diamond Syndrome
papers.label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.11.766026 v1

summary.background:
- Ribosomes build proteins; the large subunit (60S in humans) is assembled and checked in stages.
- SBDS is a protein that helps remove the factor eIF6 from the 60S subunit so that the small subunit (40S) can join and translation can start.
- Shwachman-Diamond syndrome is an inherited disorder linked to ribosome assembly defects, caused by mutations in both copies of the SBDS gene.
- Cryo-EM (cryogenic electron microscopy) freezes molecules and images them to reconstruct their three-dimensional shape at near-atomic detail.
- "Allostery" means a change at one site altering the shape or activity at a distant site.
- Key sites named: P-site, peptidyl transferase center, exit tunnel, GTPase-associated center, and the protein uL16 (RPL10).
summary.one_liner: Cryo-EM structures of human SBDS, and disease-linked SBDS variants, bound to the human 60S ribosomal subunit, showing how Shwachman-Diamond syndrome mutations disturb 60S surveillance and maturation.
summary.plain: This paper looks at a rare inherited disease, Shwachman-Diamond syndrome, which is caused by faults in a protein called SBDS. SBDS helps cells check and finish the large parts of the ribosome, the cell's protein-making machinery, before they start building proteins. The authors used high-resolution imaging to see how normal and mutated versions of SBDS sit on the ribosome, and found that the mutations disrupt contacts at several key sites and can change distant parts of the ribosome.
summary.why: It gives a structural, atom-level explanation for how specific SBDS mutations could impair ribosome quality control, which is a plausible route to the disease's bone marrow problems. The text itself does not test disease outcomes, so the link to patients is a hypothesis the structures support rather than prove.

papers.abstract: Surveillance of functional centers in the mature 60S ribosomal subunit by SBDS licenses its translational debut. Timely release of eIF6 from 60S by SBDS is essential to permit 40S joining. Biallelic mutations in SBDS associated with Shwachman-Diamond syndrome (SDS), an inherited ribosomopathy, impair dissociation of eIF6 from 60S. How SBDS variants that bind to 60S structurally perturb the maturation and surveillance of 60S is yet to be deciphered. Here, we report high-resolution cryogenic electron microscopy (cryo-EM) structures of human SBDS and pathogenic variants in complex with human 60S. The structures reveal that disease mutations disrupt key interactions of SBDS with the functional centers of the 60S subunit destabilizing critical bases and protein interactions across the P-site, peptidyl transferase center, polypeptide exit tunnel and GTPase-associated center. These mutations remodel the N-terminal contacts with 60S, altering critical interactions with uL16 (RPL10) distant from the mutation site. Mutations in domains II and III trigger conformational changes that propagate across the entirety of SBDS and remodel distant ribosomal regions, revealing an elegant mechanism of pathogenic allostery. The profound effects of SBDS mutations on both the surveillance and mature conformation of the 60S subunit provide a structural framework for understanding the molecular pathology of SDS.
